items.title: William Russell Interview, 1976-02-16
items.q: I decided to record Baby Dodds talking about drums

ctx.x: Look at all the histories of jazz that come out and barely mention Johnny Dodds. Yeah. If they mention him at all.

So I sometimes get discouraged and wonder whether it's worth fooling with trying to preserve it. One thing, project I've worked on started, though, uh, around 1950, you might say, after the Jelly Roll tapes became known, I decided to record Baby Dodds talking about drums, and, uh, I got a little, uh, book that you might say was going to publish at that time, years ago. I recorded him maybe about 12 hours talking about drums. He'd already had a couple of strokes and wasn't too effective in playing, but he could…

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-08-31
items.q: So up there in Chicago I'd interviewed Baby Dodds quite a few interviews, as well as some of his music, demonstrating the drums and different traps as they call them.

ctx.x: Well, you think that maybe it has something to do with the general environment.

Or else it's the type of people that, for one thing, one of the great principles which you can't really overemphasize in New Orleans music, in the jazz, is the working together. The way they can work together. They're all there to help one another, as they say. They'll, they're not there to steal the spotlight. They're always there trying to help somebody misses a note or they can see they're falling down on their part. They'll put in notes that'll fill in or they'll, I mean, it's not quite that simple, but I…
He was my favorite of all of them on my own record.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1975-02-02
items.q: Baby Dodds had a different theory of why the band broke up.

ctx.x: Well, of course, we'll never know what Joe Oliver really sounded like.

No, that's right. On the records, you can't tell how big his tone was. But from all the evidence, about 100% of it, you might say, of anybody that ever talked about him in the old days that heard him, talk about the big tone. That he was almost like, say, a second Bolden after Bolden, that he had that big tone. Which would have undoubtedly been bigger than Louie. However, Joe did use a lot of these freak effects, not only hats and maybe plungers and all—not so much plungers. He had this little con mute, a little…
What about— Well, anyway, I guess if there's anything else to talk about.

items.title: William Russell Interview, 1962-09-04
items.q: They probably are in a box of Baby Dodds notes, I think.

ctx.x: 1949. It says here she was approximately later, 11 years older than George Bakke. I figured that out. To get on to a few other people that I used to talk to, the next one on this list was Johnny Dodds, whose notes I'll have to send. They probably are in a box of Baby Dodds notes, I think. I was always going to try to rewrite them. When I first met Johnny Dodds about 1936, I went to Chicago and I inquired if he was playing anyplace or where he was. All I knew about him, he'd been on some of the jelly roll records…
